transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood), Maya (Stratus), Rafael (Stratus), Lena (Stratus), Tom (Stratus)

Summary (auto):
Deep dive into Stratus' KV cache eviction and paging issues when serving long-context sessions. Discussed root causes (fragmentation, prefix reuse patterns), suggested telemetry to collect, suggested config changes (cache sizing, eviction policy tuning, prefetch/pinning), and follow-ups for a benchmark run on dedicated capacity.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — i'm jordan from redwood, this is priya and carlos from our se team. how about you folks at stratus, quick intros?
[00:18] Maya: hi, i'm maya, head of ml infra at stratus. Rafael's on platform, lena handles ops, tom is the engineer seeing the kv misses.
[00:27] Jordan: great. aim of call is a technical deep dive into kv-cache eviction/paging for your long-context workloads, and figure out next steps to stabilize latency. sound right?
[00:36] Maya: yep. we've been seeing intermittent latency spikes and quality regressions on sessions > 200k tokens. we suspect kv eviction / prefix reuse thrashing.
[00:46] Priya: ok, good detail. can you walk us through your topology quickly — hosted vs dedicated, model variants, and if you're using our dedicated pool or private?
[00:56] Rafael: we're running redwood private in our vpc on prem-ish racks — it's a customer-managed deployment with the redwood control plane. we've got a dedicated GPU pool for inference (4xA100 per node) but some of the serving is on hybrid hosts.
[01:15] Tom: architecture is roughly: frontend API -> batcher -> runtime per-GPU shards -> kv cache per-shard backed by local nvme. we do LRU-ish eviction.
[01:27] Priya: good. what are your typical sequence lengths and batch shapes?
[01:31] Tom: average is 8k tokens, heavy tail up to 350k tokens for some analyst sessions. bursty concurrency — 30 concurrent sessions at peak. batch sizes are small for long-context sessions, often 1-4.
[01:45] Carlos: mmm that heavy tail is the trick. long-context sessions keep kv entries per token in memory, so eviction/paging becomes a function of both working set size and prefix reuse. when you have many unique prefixes, the cache doesn't get much reuse.
[01:59] Lena: we're seeing nvme paging too — the runtime tries to spill to disk but we get huge seek latency spikes causing downstream 2-3s tail tokens.
[02:10] Priya: are you using prefix reuse across sessions? i.e. are users frequently reusing the same initial prompt prefixes or are these unique chat histories?
[02:18] Maya: mix. some customers use templated prompts (good prefix reuse), others have dynamic contexts (less reuse). we suspect the spikes correlate with low-prefix-reuse sessions.
[02:30] Priya: ok, so two main problems possible: 1) working set exceeds in-memory kv capacity causing frequent eviction and disk paging, and 2) prefix conflicts or near-duplicates preventing effective cache hits (prefix reuse issue). both lead to tail latencies and sometimes quality regressions if kv entries get evicted mid-generation.
[02:51] Tom: also we saw eviction patterns where older prefixes get evicted even though later tokens still reference them — feels like fragmentation.
[02:58] Carlos: fragmentation can happen when the runtime stores per-key metadata and the eviction is based on global LRU counters. if you have many small sessions interleaved, the LRU can evict entries that are still logically in-use by long sessions because of timestamp aliasing.
[03:15] Priya: couple questions — what eviction policy are you using? LRU, seg-lru, or something like FIFO? and do you have pinning for pinned prefixes?
[03:24] Rafael: default is LRU. we haven't implemented pinning yet.
[03:28] Priya: ok that explains some of it. we recommend: seg-LRU or generational LRU to protect hot prefixes, and add explicit pinning for known-long sessions (e.g., conversation anchors). also consider a small in-memory metadata heap to avoid fragmentation of nvme-backed entries.
[03:45] Maya: pinning sounds promising — but how do we choose what to pin? we can't pin everything.
[03:51] Priya: pick the high-value prefix classes: templated system prompts, frequent user templates, and any prompt segments used for reranking/recall. You can also implement a heuristic: anything with hit-rate > X over Y minutes becomes pinned.
[04:06] Tom: about paging — we run nvme in Q2. it's pretty fast but tails are bad. is there an option to do async prefetch?
[04:13] Carlos: yes, runtime supports async prefetch of KV pages based on predicted token horizon. the kicker is accuracy of prediction. for long sessions with small batch sizes you can prefetch next N pages when generation starts and keep them resident. tradeoff is memory pressure.
[04:27] Priya: another lever is to compress cached KV values via quantization — for example 4-bit quantization on KV values reduces footprint allowing longer retention. but that can slightly affect logits fidelity for some models.
[04:40] Maya: we were worried quantization might break downstream quality for our summarization pipeline. any numbers?
[04:45] Carlos: in our internal tests with LlamaX variants, 4-bit on KV vectors gave ~12% memory reduction with <0.5% perplexity change in most completion workloads. for extreme long-context reasoning it can cause small drift; we can recommend a per-workload A/B.
[05:00] Rafael: could batching changes help? our long sessions force batch size 1 often.
[05:05] Priya: batching helps throughput but for latency-sensitive long streams it's tricky. hybrid: keep micro-batching for short sessions but allow asynchronous KV writeback batching for long sessions so eviction decisions see consolidated access patterns. also consider bucketed routing by seq-length to avoid mixing short and ultra-long sessions on the same shard; that reduces churn.
[05:26] Tom: bucketed routing — interesting. that would mean we need to tag session seq-length and route to a dedicated pool?
[05:31] Carlos: exactly. route long-context sessions to nodes with larger KV capacity and adjusted eviction parameters. reduces interference.
[05:39] Maya: we have dedicated nodes already but they still show eviction when concurrent long sessions spike. maybe our cache sizing is underspecified. what are the heuristics for sizing kv cache relative to expected token horizon?
[05:52] Priya: good question. rough heuristic: in-memory KV bytes = expected concurrent long-session working set * average per-token KV size * safety factor (1.5-2x). per-token KV size depends on model (hidden_dim*2 bytes for FP16, or smaller with quantization). if you expect 20 sessions at 200k tokens each, that's huge, so you either need eviction/pinning strategy or shard isolation.
[06:17] Lena: our NVMe is 4TB per node but we prefer memory to avoid seek tails. should we just add more RAM?
[06:23] Priya: adding RAM helps but is costy. better to combine: route ultra-long sessions to nodes with larger memory, use pinning for top prefixes, use seg-LRU to protect hot keys, and quantize cold keys. Also TTL-based eviction for ephemeral prefixes (e.g., system prompts that are rarely accessed after x minutes).
[06:44] Maya: quick note — some of our customers do prefix reuse where they include the whole conversation history as repeated system/meta. that makes prefixes extremely large. is prefix deduping a thing?
[06:55] Carlos: yes, prefix deduplication and normalization are effective. canonicalize prefixes and store references to a shared representation in the kv store — reduces duplication. it's an engineering lift but big wins for reuse-heavy workloads.
[07:08] Tom: on the spike incidents, we captured heap stats and some eviction logs. attaching a snippet here: (they pasted). the logs show rapid churn: evict event rates up to 10k/sec during peaks.
[07:21] Priya: that churn rate is consistent with hash-thrashing. did you see many small objects being evicted vs fewer large objects?
[07:27] Tom: mostly small objects — lots of small prefix segments.
[07:30] Priya: that suggests sticky small-prefix churn. strategies: increase granularity of keys so that you can evict larger segments atomically, or change insertion policy to coalesce prefix segments into larger blobs with reference counts. both are code changes but can reduce metadata housekeeping.
[07:47] Rafael: what's the recommended eviction policy change if we can't re-architect quickly? something we can flip at runtime?
[07:54] Priya: switch to a two-tier cache with a small hot in-memory tier and a larger warm tier on nvme with async migration. On eviction you first demote to warm tier instead of full delete — that reduces expensive disk reads for re-hits. Also lower the LRU sensitivity window to prefer recent items.
[08:11] Carlos: we can provide a drop-in config patch for the warm-tier demotion and seg-lru parameters for testing.
[08:17] Maya: that'd be helpful. also, what telemetry should we send you to help root cause?
[08:22] Priya: send: eviction logs (evict event with key size, reason, timestamp), kv hit/miss heatmaps by prefix, per-shard memory utilization, NVMe IO tail latency percentiles, and example session ids for which quality regressed. also config: eviction policy, kv sizes, quantization profiles.
[08:41] Tom: we can supply those. question — is there a way to correlate quality regressions to specific kv evictions? we're seeing hallucination bursts aligned with eviction times.
[08:50] Carlos: yes, correlate generation traces with eviction timestamps and token indexes. if a required KV entry is evicted right before it's referenced, you'll see a higher probability of token drift. We can instrument generation to log reference misses and attach them to the session trace.
[09:06] Priya: two quick mitigations to prove concept: 1) for sessions with known critical accuracy, pin the essential prefixes; 2) enable async prefetch + warm-tier demotion for a subset of traffic and compare error rates.
[09:20] Maya: ok. timeline?
[09:23] Jordan: immediate: we'll share the trace tool and suggested config. next week we'll reconvene after they upload logs and we run a basic sim. then schedule a 1-day on-site/remote bench run mid-next week.
[09:33] Rafael: one more question — VPC/networking. sometimes the control plane sends backfill requests and we see bursty flows. could that cause churn?
[09:41] Carlos: yes, control-plane routing changes (e.g., model fallback) can create temporal spikes. ensure your routing policy avoids mass-fallbacks during outages. set gradual rollouts / canary to avoid synchronized backfills.
[09:54] Tom: what about quantization tradeoffs? if we quantize KV only but keep weights in higher precision, is that supported?
[10:01] Priya: yes. KV-only quantization is common: it reduces memory but keeps model weights intact. Redwood runtime supports per-buffer quant schemes. Test per-model.
[10:10] Maya: for experimental purposes, what kind of latency improvement should we target?
[10:14] Carlos: depends, but with pinning + seg-LRU + warm-tier demotion you can reduce tail token latency by 30-60% on eviction-driven spikes. Quantization gives capacity improvements allowing fewer evictions, so indirectly reduces tails too.
[10:29] Tom: we want to try the warm-tier demotion first, then quantize cold entries.
[10:34] Priya: sounds good. i'll send a recommended config diff. Also we'll include a small script to collect the eviction events and a sample number of sessions to run a controlled benchmark.
[10:44] Maya: how would we run a bench with your SE? do you need access to our staging cluster or you can run against a captured workload?
[10:51] Carlos: both options work. capture workload is lower friction: provide captured request traces + model weights/config and we can simulate. If you prefer live runs, we can coordinate remote access with read-only telemetry and a scheduled window.
[11:06] Rafael: we'll start with captured traces. i'll prepare them and the env config.
[11:11] Jordan: perfect. quick recap and owners?
[11:14] Maya: recap please.
[11:16] Jordan: recap: 1) Redwood to share kv-cache trace tool and warm-tier config (Priya/Carlos) 2) Stratus to upload eviction logs, session traces, and model config (Maya/Rafael/Tom) 3) SE to run preliminary sim and return latency/cost matrix (Carlos) 4) schedule follow up bench the week of 2026-11-16.
[11:37] Priya: small note — consider enabling prefix canonicalization in your ingest pipeline; we'll send example code.
[11:44] Tom: great. any other blockers?
[11:47] Lena: security question: we'll need an NDA/scan for config sharing and SSO for access if live runs needed.
[11:53] Jordan: noted. we'll share security docs (SOC2, SAML guide) and a limited-access onboarding checklist.
[12:01] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll aim to get artifacts up by Thursday.
[12:05] Jordan: thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links. bye.
